questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: First of all, I wanted to explore a destination with both different culture and nature compared to Copenhagen. I was very much dragged to the outdoor opportunities such as skiing, climbing, and hiking and wanted to explore what it's like attending a university with a large campus and a vibrant campus life. Furthermore, I was under the impression that the academic level was quite good and expected having some very interesting classes.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: In terms of classes getting the information was quite difficult. It was not possible choosing any courses beforehand and I had to show up and ask professors in person if I could attend the classes. Luckily, I ended up getting all the courses I was hoping for. Regarding practicalities it was quite easy since UBC has a lot of experience with both exchange students and new students in general that need a lot of information since many students travel to UBC from abroad.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received assistance from the professors at the political science department and the department for public policy and global affairs regarding how to enroll in the courses. Regarding housing, I received a lot of information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I could really have used additional assistance on how to enroll in political science and public policy and global affairs courses because I felt like I was a lot on my own in terms of seeking the required information - especially since I needed my credits transferred to 30 ECTS points which created a lot of uncertainty before and the first weeks after my arrival.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I was staying in a unit with five other students on campus. I think studios were available as well.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: We had our own kitchen in our unit which the six of us shared.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Future Danish exchange students should know that most other students are a bit younger and less used to living on their own. I experienced different standards of cleaning etc. which has to be dealt with for everyone to feel at home in the unit. With that said, staying in a shared unit on campus was one of my greatest experiences during my exchange, regardless of different perceptions of how to keep the unit clean and tidy.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The only thing I could have wished for was additional help regarding clarifying cleaning standards. This was very much up to ourselves which I think is ok since we're all grown ups, however to make sure the unit was tidy enough to live in I had to put quite some effort into coordinating cleaning schedules etc.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I received very little information on course registration both before and after my arrival. This is because I had to attend graduate courses to get my credits transferred, but through the official system I could only enroll in undergraduate courses. This meant that I had to attend classes I was not registered for and ask the professors in political science and public policy and global affairs for permission to attend their courses. This proved to be no problem but resulted in a lot of stress before and the first weeks of my exchange. I could have hoped for better assistance from both UCPH and UBC. However, it is possible to register and drop courses the first two weeks of the term at UBC which was a necessity for me to enroll in any graduate courses at all and also really great so that I could try out different courses and enroll in the ones I liked the most, since I only had to attend three courses.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to register for undergraduate courses beforehand, but I knew I wouldn't attend any of those since I got the impression that these could not get transferred to ECTS credits in my master study at UCPH. This meant I had to show up and address the graduate professors in person and ask for permission to attend their classes. After their permission, there was no problem with attending the graduate courses. However, it was possible for graduate students at UBC to register in the courses beforehand which meant that certain courses had extensive waiting lists, so I was lucky that the professors understood my special situation and allowed me to skip the waiting list.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I couldn't find any general help regarding figuring out my possibilities of enrolling in the graduate courses. I had to see the graduate professors in person to enroll.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful and registered in all classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: In political science and public policy and global affairs, I would enroll in undergraduate courses because this is what is needed in UBC's system. I would look into graduate courses and write professors of interest beforehand, explaining your special situation. Then I would show up to all potential classes the first week of classes and talk to the professors about the possibility of enrolling in their course. I would enroll in enough courses to make sure that you can get the credits transferred to 30 ECTS points and then I would drop some excess courses before the deadline.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found that the level was varying at the courses, but all of the classes were interesting. However, all of the classes had fewer students attending that I'm used to and in all courses it was expected to participate actively at classes and to hand in assignments during the term. It was possible for me to participate with my academic and English level but I had to get used to the expectation of active participation which varies a lot from UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The classes had fewer students and it was expected to participate actively at classes and hand in assignments throughout the term which is not expected at UCPH. I also found that the relationship between the professors and students was closer and that the professors were very interested in the student's papers which was very nice.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Gender, Peace and Security (Public Policy and Global Affairs)
Topics in Political Theory: Contested Territory (Political Science)
Human Rights and the Environment (Public Policy and Global Affairs)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would highly recommend Topics in Political Theory: Contested Territory (Political Science) and Human Rights and the Environment (Public Policy and Global Affairs). Contested Territory was political theory which included a lot of knowledge on indigenous people in general and in Canada and the US specifically which is not something I have found on syllabuses in UCPH and the professor, Anna Jurkevics, was very engaged in the topic. Human Rights and the Environment is also highly recommendable, since it had a multidisciplinary approach to human rights from an environmental point of view and the professor, David Boyd, is the UN special rapporteur on human rights and the environment and had extensive knowledge within the field and is very inspiring.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to pay for all of my rent beforehand, some time during January.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Grocery shopping in Vancouver was more expensive than I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UBC has a wide range of non-academic opportunities. Personally, I joined the outdoor club, climbing club and dancing club. I think there are all clubs available one can possibly imagine.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were multiple social activities available through my housing offer such as hiking trips, crafts, and parties. Furthermore there are all kinds of athletic activities, including a free aquatic center at campus.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would highly recommend joining the climbing club, the Aviary, since it is cheep and people are very friendly and its very conveniently located at campus. Furthermore the outdoor club, VOC, arranges different outdoor trips which is a good way to explore the nature as a newcomer. Also I enjoyed joining the dancing club where I attended a hip hop team and performed at a show at the end of the term and furthermore had the opportunity to join other dancing classes throughout the term.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would highly recommend buying a season pass for Whistler skiing resort with student discount. I skied the whole term for around 3000 DKK and rented gear for the season and there are busses driving back and forth from Vancouver to Whistler and a lot of people also shared rented cars for day or weekend trips. This is my number one recommendation. Apart from that there are multiple hiking opportunities around Vancouver that are exceptional experiences.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think it was quite alright. UBC and Vancouver is highly multicultural compared to UCPH and Copenhagen which was a big experience. This meant that most people were quite different from myself and gave me many new experiences.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I would join clubs and different events for students in general or exchange students specifically.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Mostly that people in general were quite different from myself and you have to prepare to meet and socialize in different circumstances than you're probably used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Mostly that people came from many different cultural backgrounds and brought new perspectives and things to do together.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Make sure to attend a lot of events and join a lot of clubs. Make sure to take advantage of the outdoors such as skiing or hiking. And I would highly recommend staying in a shared unit in campus to have an everyday with people you probably wouldn't meet if you didn't.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Staying in a shared flat with other students and learning about their lives and culture which was very different from my own.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I think the greatest challenge was socializing with people quite different from myself who have other ways of life.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
